Here are verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 9, drawing on the sources I was able to consult. I could not access everything due to tool limits, so what follows is what the pages actually say. Where a tradition or viewpoint is absent below, it is because I could not find or fetch a relevant source within the constraints.

---

## Isaiah 9:1–7 — The Promise of Light and the Messianic King

### v. 1: “Nevertheless, there will be no more gloom for those in distress…”

**Traditional reading:** This verse begins by contrasting with the gloom of Isaiah 8:22. The northern territories — Zebulun and Naphtali — had been devastated by the Assyrian invasions under Tiglath-Pileser III (2 Kings 15:29). God “humbled” or “lightly esteemed” them in judgment. But the promise is that this same despised region would later be specially honoured. The “Way of the Sea” refers to the district around the Sea of Galilee (the Via Maris trade route). “Galilee of the nations/Gentiles” reflects the mixed Jewish-Gentile population of that border region.

— Enduring Word (David Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (Ellicott notes “the word Galilee, derived from the same root as Gilgal, means strictly ‘a circle,’ or ‘circuit.’”)

— Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_9_commentary (adds that after the Assyrian deportation, Gentiles were resettled there, making it a “melting pot” and explaining the name “Galilee of the Gentiles.”)

— Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-9.html (notes the Jews in these parts were “mean and illiterate, not famous for any arts or sciences, and having no prophet among them” — yet would be honoured by Messiah’s presence.)

**NT fulfilment:** Matthew 4:13–16 explicitly quotes Isaiah 9:1–2 as fulfilled when Jesus moved to Capernaum and ministered in Galilee.

— Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_9_commentary

---

### v. 2: “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light…”

**Traditional reading:** The “darkness” is spiritual darkness — living without knowledge of God. The “great light” is the Messiah Himself. Matthew 4:16 applies this directly to Jesus’ Galilean ministry. The Hebrew verbs are in the perfect tense (“have seen,” “has dawned”), what scholars call the “prophetic perfect” — future events so certain they are described as if already accomplished.

— Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_9_commentary

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (adds the nuance that Isaiah was probably thinking of Assyrian invasions and national restoration, and Matthew “adapts the words of prophecy to a further meaning than that which apparently was in the mind of the writer.”)

— Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-9.html (identifies “the people that walked in darkness” as “the inhabitants of Galilee in the times of Christ” and elaborates on spiritual darkness as “a state of darkness, under the power of sin, shut up in unbelief.”)

**“Land of the shadow of death”:** The phrase echoes Psalm 23:4 and Job 3:5, picturing a grim, hopeless state — almost like Sheol itself — before Messiah’s light breaks in.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

---

### v. 3: “You have enlarged the nation and increased its joy…”

**Traditional reading:** The “nation” is understood as spiritual Israel — those who believe. The joy is compared to harvest joy (the peaceful, grateful joy of gathering crops) and to warriors dividing spoil (the triumphant joy of victory). The words “before You” are significant — this is joy in God’s presence, like worshippers at a feast. The KJV reads “and not increased the joy,” following the written Hebrew text (the *Ketiv*); but the marginal reading (the *Qere*) says “increased joy *to it*,” which nearly all modern translations and commentators follow.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

— Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-9.html (explains the *Ketiv/Qere* issue in detail and notes the “joy” is spiritual joy at conversion and at beholding Christ by faith.)

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/ (Guzik compares the joy to “the locker room of a championship team.”)

---

### v. 4: “For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke…”

**Traditional reading:** The “yoke,” “bar,” and “rod” represent oppression — the ceremonial law, the tyranny of Satan, and the dominion of sin. “The day of Midian” refers to Gideon’s miraculous victory over the Midianites in Judges 7, where a tiny, unarmed force won by God’s power alone. The point is that Messiah’s victory, like Gideon’s, comes through divine power, not human might. The deliverance is from spiritual bondage — sin, Satan, and law — not merely political oppression.

— Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-9.html

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“Of all victories in the history of Israel, that of Gideon over the Midianites had been most conspicuous for this feature… Men remembered ‘the day of Midian’ centuries after its date, as we remember Poitiers and Agincourt.”)

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/ (Guzik applies this to the believer’s spiritual victory in Christ: “As we are in Jesus Christ, we share in His victory.”)

---

### v. 5: “For every trampling boot of battle and every garment rolled in blood will be burned…”

**Traditional reading:** All the instruments of war — the soldier’s heavy boot, blood-soaked cloaks — will be consigned to the fire because they are no longer needed. The battle is decisively won, and peace has come. This pictures the complete cessation of hostilities that accompanies Messiah’s reign. Some note that it was customary after victory to burn the enemy’s armour and spoils, so there would be no more war.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“The victory is decisive, and the reign of peace begins, and the weapons of war… these shall all be burnt up.”)

— Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_9_commentary (“How will Jehovah put an end to ‘the yoke’? … by putting an end to wars! … This can only transpire with the return of the Prince of peace.”)

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/ (“the battle is over. This is what you did when the battle was finished, and you had won.”)

---

### v. 6: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given…”

This is the heart of the chapter and the most debated verse in terms of translation and theology.

#### The Two-Nature Christology

**Traditional reading (all major Protestant traditions):** “A child is born” points to Jesus’ true humanity — He had a birth, a beginning as man. “A son is given” points to His eternal deity — the Son is the eternal Second Person of the Trinity, “given” from heaven, not born into existence. Together they confess the incarnation: fully God and fully man.

— Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/ (“without humanity He couldn’t be our substitute; without deity His sacrifice would be insufficient.”)

— Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-9.html (the child is born “for us, for our good, for our profit and advantage… that he might be a fit Mediator and Redeemer.”)

#### The Names / Titles

**How many names?** This is a point of genuine disagreement. The traditional KJV and many conservative Protestants read five separate titles: “Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.” But many scholars argue for four titles, joining “Wonderful Counsellor” into one: (1) Wonderful Counsellor, (2) Mighty God, (3) Everlasting Father, (4) Prince of Peace. Ellicott argues for this four-title reading because the last six Hebrew words “obviously fall into three couplets,” so the first two words should be paired as well.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“It is probable that the first two should also be taken together, and that we have four elements of the compound name.”)

**“Wonderful Counselor”:** The Hebrew *pele’* (“wonderful”) carries overtones of deity (cf. Judges 13:18 where the Angel of the LORD’s name is “wonderful”). The Messiah is a wonder, and His counsel is divine, faithful, and sweet. Spurgeon (quoted at length in Enduring Word) preached that just as a counsellor (Satan in the serpent) ruined the world, so a Counsellor restores it.

— Enduring Word (Guzik, quoting Spurgeon): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

**“Mighty God”:** The Hebrew is *’El Gibbor*. The word *’El* is significant — it is not *Elohim* (which can sometimes refer to human judges or rulers), but *’El*, which in Isaiah “is never used hyperbolically or metaphorically” but always denotes “divinity in an absolute sense” (Pulpit Commentary). In Isaiah 10:21, the exact phrase *’El Gibbor* is used of Yahweh Himself. This is the classic proof-text for the full deity of the Messiah.

— Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/9.htm

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“It is significant that the word for ‘God’ is not Elohim … but El, which is never used by Isaiah … in any lower sense than that of absolute Deity.”)

— Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/ (“It is difficult to think of a more straightforward declaration of the deity of the Messiah.” He notes Jehovah’s Witnesses try to distinguish “Mighty God” from “Almighty God,” but Revelation 1:8 applies “Almighty” to Jesus.)

**NET Bible notes (alternative view):** Some modern scholars argue that in its original context, *’El Gibbor* portrays the Davidic king as God’s representative on the battlefield, whom God empowers — not as a statement of ontological deity. They cite Egyptian and ancient Near Eastern parallels where kings are described in divine terms. However, the NET notes acknowledge that the use of this same title for Yahweh in Isaiah 10:21 “supports” the interpretation of actual deity, and that the New Testament indicates the hyperbolic language is “literally realized in the ultimate fulfillment.”

— NET Bible: https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Isa+9%3A6%2C7 (accessed via search results; the full page could not be fetched.)

**“Everlasting Father”:** Traditional reading: This does *not* mean the Messiah is the Person of the Father in the Trinity (that would be modalistic). Rather, “Father” describes His character toward His people — a fatherly protector, provider, and author of eternal life. The Hebrew *’avi-‘ad* means “Father of Eternity.” He is the source or possessor of eternity, the Creator. Ellicott notes another rendering, “Father of the age to come,” found in the LXX and Vulgate.

— Spurgeon, “His Name—the Everlasting Father” (summary from search result): https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/his-name-the-everlasting-father (“The Messiah is not here called ‘Father,’ by way of any confusion with him who is pre-eminently called ‘THE FATHER.’ … Our text … does not indicate the relation of Deity to itself, but the relation of Jesus Christ to us.”)

— Benson’s Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-9.html (“The Father of eternity … Christ … is the God and Father of all things … and especially the Father of all believers.”)

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (he uses “Father of Eternity” and notes that “none other expressed so well the true idea of loving and protecting government.”)

**NET Bible alternative view:** The title could be royal hyperbole in its original context — like a Phoenician inscription where a ruler is called “a father and a mother” to his people — emphasizing the king’s protective role and long reign, not literal deity or eternality. The NT shows the hyperbole becomes literal in Christ.

— NET Bible (search result): https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Isa+9%3A6%2C7

**“Prince of Peace”:** The Messiah brings peace between God and man, and ultimately peace on earth. This title gathers up all the war-ending imagery from vv. 4–5.

— Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“The prophet clings, as all prophets before him had done, to the thought that peace, and not war, belonged to the ideal Kingdom of the Messiah.”)

#### Denominational Distinctives on v. 6

- **Reformed / Calvinist:** Emphasise the sovereignty of the titles — Christ is Mighty God, His government is absolute. Calvin (quoted by Guzik): “If Christ were not the Son of God, his death, so far from being a satisfaction for sin, was a death most richly and righteously deserved.” Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist) strongly defended the full deity of Christ from this verse against Unitarian denials.
- **Lutheran:** Luther emphasised God’s use of opposites — the Mighty God lying in a manger, clad in diapers — to reveal Himself. https://www.1517.org/articles/behold-the-king-israel-never-expected
- **Pentecostal / Charismatic:** David Guzik (Enduring Word) applies all the titles as present-tense realities for believers who “receive Jesus and submit to Him,” not merely future hopes.
- **Jehovah’s Witnesses (noted by Guzik):** They try to distinguish “Mighty God” (*’El Gibbor*) from “Almighty God” (*’El Shaddai*), but Guzik notes the phrase appears of Yahweh in Isaiah 10:21 and “Almighty” is applied to Jesus in Revelation 1:8.

---

### v. 7: “Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end…”

**Traditional reading:** Messiah’s kingdom will grow without limit and endure forever. He will sit on “the throne of David” — a fulfilment of the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7). The kingdom is established and sustained “with justice and righteousness.” The final clause — “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this” — means God’s passionate commitment (the Hebrew root can mean both “zeal” and “jealousy”) guarantees the fulfilment.

— Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/9.htm

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“It is because Jehovah loves the daughter of Zion with an absorbing love that He purposes such great things for her future.”)

— Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/ (notes a millennial understanding: “Jesus will rule on David’s throne … a fulfillment of God’s great covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7.”)

**Dispensational / Premillennial view:** The “throne of David” refers to a literal, future, earthly reign of Christ from Jerusalem during the Millennium, followed by the eternal state. “The increase of His government” will unfold during that earthly reign.

— Enduring Word (Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/

— Precept Austin (Constable): https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_9_commentary (“the Lord would raise up a faithful King … referring to Jesus at His return as King of kings.”)

**Amillennial / Covenant Theology view:** The “throne of David” is fulfilled in Christ’s present heavenly session at the right hand of the Father. His kingdom is spiritual, now expanding through the gospel, and will be consummated at His return in the new heavens and new earth — without a distinct literal millennium.

(I was unable to fetch a dedicated Reformed amillennial source on Isaiah 9:7 within the tool limits, but this represents a well-known distinction in Protestant eschatology.)

**Catholic and Orthodox views:** I was unable to fetch Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) pages on Isaiah 9 within the tool limits. The StudyLight summary page for Isaiah 9:6 notes that among 61 commentators, 1 was Catholic. The traditional Catholic reading (as seen in the LXX/Vulgate tradition) reads “the Angel of Great Counsel” for “Wonderful Counsellor” and “Father of the age to come” for “Everlasting Father,” and strongly affirms the messianic and divine character of the passage. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/9-6.html)

## Isaiah 9:8–21 — Judgment on the Northern Kingdom

This section (Isaiah 9:8–10:4) is structured as a poem in four stanzas, each ending with the refrain: “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised” (vv. 12, 17, 21, and 10:4). Some call it “The Speech of the Outstretched Hand.”

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

---

### vv. 8–12 — First Stanza: Pride and Defiance

**v. 8:** “The Lord has sent a message against Jacob, and it has fallen upon Israel.”

The “word” is the prophetic message of judgment. Ellicott notes that “Jacob” and “Israel” probably both refer to Judah as the true representative of Israel, while the northern kingdom is called merely “Ephraim” (as in Isaiah 7:5, 8, 17) — the apostate ten tribes being no longer worthy of the name “Israel.”

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

**vv. 9–10:** The pride of Ephraim and Samaria is expressed in defiant building metaphors: even if cheap brick houses fall, they will rebuild with expensive hewn stone; if humble sycamore wood is destroyed, they will replace it with costly cedar. They boast that they can recover from any disaster by their own resources.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“Sun-dried bricks and the cheap timber of the sycamore were the common materials used for the dwellings of the poor, hewn stones and cedar for the palaces of the rich.”)

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/ (“We either bow down to the Lord in worship now, or we will bow down without Him in suffering and humiliation later.”)

**vv. 11–12:** In response, the LORD raises up “the foes of Rezin” (the Assyrians who had already conquered Syria) against Ephraim. Aram (Syria) from the east and Philistia from the west will “devour Israel with open mouths.” Ellicott explains the irony: Syria, having been conquered by Assyria, was now compelled to fight *against* Samaria — the very people they had previously allied with.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

**“Despite all this, His anger is not turned away…”:** This refrain means that even these severe judgments do not exhaust God’s wrath. The outstretched hand is not a hand of welcome but a hand poised to strike again. The repetition underscores persistent, unrelenting judgment on impenitence.

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-9/

---

### vv. 13–17 — Second Stanza: Refusal to Repent and Leadership Failure

**v. 13:** “But the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts.” The core problem: not just sin, but impenitence. They were struck but would not turn.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

**vv. 14–15:** “Head and tail, palm branch and reed” is a proverbial expression for the entire leadership structure — from the highest to the lowest. The “head” is the elder and honourable man (the civil and social leaders). The “tail” is “the prophet who teaches lies” — the false religious leaders. All will be cut off “in a single day,” indicating sudden, comprehensive judgment.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“to Isaiah, as to Jeremiah, there was no class so contemptible and base as that of spiritual guides whose policy was that of a time-serving selfishness.”)

**v. 16:** The leaders mislead; those led are “swallowed up” or “destroyed.” Both the deceivers and the deceived face judgment.

**v. 17:** So universal is the corruption that even those who normally arouse God’s compassion — young men, orphans, widows — receive no pity. “Every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly” (Ellicott: “blasphemy or villainy”). The second refrain closes the stanza.

---

### vv. 18–21 — Third Stanza: Social Collapse and Civil War

**vv. 18–19:** Wickedness is compared to a forest fire — it starts with thorns and briers (the lowly and worthless) and then kindles the forest thickets (the whole society), sending up billows of smoke. “By the wrath of the LORD of Hosts the land is scorched, and the people are fuel for the fire.” Sin becomes its own punishment.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“sin becomes the punishment of sin, and burns like a fire in a forest thicket.”)

**v. 20:** The image shifts from fire to cannibalism — intense internal strife and self-destruction. People “carve out” food to the right and left but are never satisfied. “Each one devours the flesh of his own offspring” (BSB: “his own offspring”; lit. “the flesh of his own arm,” meaning his own kin or tribal brothers). Ellicott connects this to the horrors of siege famine (cf. 2 Kings 6:28–29) but sees it primarily as figurative for the chaos tearing society apart.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm

**v. 21:** Manasseh and Ephraim — the two leading tribes of the northern kingdom, both sons of Joseph — devour each other, old tribal jealousies breaking into open conflict (cf. Judges 8:1; 12:1–4; 2 Samuel 19:43). “Together they turn against Judah” — the only unity they can muster is their common hostility to the Davidic throne. This had its historical expression in the Syro-Ephraimite alliance of Pekah and Rezin (2 Chronicles 28:6–15). The third refrain closes the stanza.

— Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/9.htm (“The only power of union that showed itself in the northern kingdom was to perpetuate the great schism in which it had its origin.”)

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Differences (where found)

| Issue | View | Source |
|-------|------|--------|
| Number of titles in v. 6 | Five (KJV, many conservatives): Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace | Gill, Pulpit |
| | Four: Wonderful Counsellor (joined), Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace | Ellicott |
| “Mighty God” = ontological deity? | Yes — *’El* never used hyperbolically in Isaiah | Pulpit, Ellicott, Guzik |
| | Possibly royal hyperbole in original context; deity only in NT fulfilment | NET Bible notes |
| “Everlasting Father” | Does not confuse Persons; means “Father of eternity” or protector of his people | Spurgeon, Benson, Ellicott |
| “Throne of David” | Literal future millennial reign | Guzik (dispensational/Pentecostal) |
| | Present heavenly reign; amillennial fulfilment | Reformed covenant theology (not fetched) |
| Lutheran emphasis | God reveals Himself in opposites — the Mighty God in a manger | 1517.org |
| Jehovah’s Witnesses | “Mighty God” ≠ “Almighty God” (refuted by Guzik using Rev 1:8) | Noted by Enduring Word |
